where: Section 3 (configuration, compatibility and internationalisation), currency example
problem: The text says “The same amount is ₹1,23,456.78 in India and $123,456.78 in the US.” The digit strings are the same, but the amounts are not: ₹1,23,456.78 is roughly a thousand times smaller than $123,456.78. A student can read this as 1 rupee = 1 dollar. What the example is really showing is grouping (lakh style vs thousand style) and the currency symbol, not an equal amount.
fix: “The same number is grouped ₹1,23,456.78 in India (lakh grouping: 1,23,456) and 123,456.78 in the US (thousand grouping). The currency symbol is also part of the locale; the actual amount depends on the exchange rate.”

problem: Calling internationalisation testing “grouped under configuration testing” is loose. It is a separate type of non-functional test that this chapter happens to place in the same section; it is not a subset of configuration testing.
fix: “Internationalisation (i18n) testing checks currency, number and date formats for each locale. This chapter covers it in the same section as configuration testing, but it is a separate type of test.”

problem: The split “a performance test runs at expected load; a load test runs at the expected peak” is not the standard textbook split. Most syllabi use performance testing as the umbrella term, with load testing one of its types: running the system at anticipated load, including peak load.
fix: “Performance testing is the umbrella term for measuring speed and capacity under a stated workload. Within it, load testing runs the system at the anticipated load, including the expected peak such as 10,000 virtual users; stress testing (Section 2) goes beyond that peak.”
